content: \chaplabel{scapegoat} In this chapter, we study a binary search tree data structure, the ScapegoatTree. This structure is based on the common wisdom that, when something goes wrong, the first thing people tend to do is find someone to blame (the \emph{scapegoat}). \index{scapegoat} Once blame is firmly established, we can leave the scapegoat to fix the problem. A ScapegoatTree keeps itself balanced by \emph{partial rebuilding operations}. \index{partial rebuilding} \index{binary search tree!partial rebuilding} During a partial rebuilding operation, an entire subtree is deconstructed and rebuilt into a perfectly balanced subtree. There are many ways of rebuilding a subtree rooted at node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} into a perfectly balanced tree. One of the simplest is to traverse \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s subtree, gathering all its nodes into an array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}, and then to recursively build a balanced subtree using \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}. If we let $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}}}=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}/2$, then the element \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}]}} becomes the root of the new subtree, $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}[0],\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}}}-1]$ get stored recursively in the left subtree and $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}}}+1],\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}-1]$ get stored recursively in the right subtree.

In this chapter, we study a binary search tree data structure, the
ScapegoatTree.  This structure is based on the common wisdom that,
when something goes wrong, the first thing people tend to do is find
someone to blame (the \emph{scapegoat}).
\index{scapegoat}%
Once blame is firmly
established, we can leave the scapegoat to fix the problem.
A ScapegoatTree keeps itself balanced by \emph{partial rebuilding
operations}.
\index{partial rebuilding}%
\index{binary search tree!partial rebuilding}%
During a partial rebuilding operation, an entire subtree is
deconstructed and rebuilt into a perfectly balanced subtree.  There are
many ways of rebuilding a subtree rooted at node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} into a perfectly
balanced tree.  One of the simplest is to traverse \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s subtree,
gathering all its nodes into an array, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}, and then to recursively
build a balanced subtree using \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}.  If we let $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}}}=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}/2$,
then the element \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}[\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}]}} becomes the root of the new subtree,
$\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}[0],\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}}}-1]$ get stored recursively in the left subtree
and $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{m}}}}+1],\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{a}}}}[\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{length}(\ensuremath{\mathit{a}})}}-1]$ get stored recursively in the
right subtree.

content: The cost of rebuilding the scapegoat node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}, once we find it, is $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{size}(\ensuremath{\mathit{w}})}})$. When searching for the scapegoat node, we call \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{size}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} on a sequence of nodes $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_0,\ldots,\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_k$ until we find the scapegoat $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_k=\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{w}}}}$. Therefore, the cost of all calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{size}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} is \begin{eqnarray*} O\left( \sum_{i=0}^k \ensuremath{\ensuremath{size}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_{k-i}\ensuremath{)} \right) &=& O\left( \ensuremath{\ensuremath{size}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_k\ensuremath{)} + \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{size}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_{k-i-1}\ensuremath{)} \right) \\ &=& O\left( \ensuremath{\ensuremath{size}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_k\ensuremath{)} + \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^i\ensuremath{\ensuremath{size}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_{k}\ensuremath{)} \right) \\ &=& O\left( \ensuremath{\ensuremath{size}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_k\ensuremath{)}\left(1+ \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^i \right)\right) \\ &=& O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{size}(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}_k\ensuremath{)}) = O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{size}(\ensuremath{\mathit{w}})}}) \enspace , \end{eqnarray*} where the last line follows from the fact that the sum is a geometrically decreasing series.

The scheme gives out a total of $O(m\log m)$ credits and every call to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{rebuild}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} is paid for with credits stored at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. During an insertion or deletion, we give one credit to each node on the path to the inserted node, or deleted node, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}. In this way we hand out at most $\log_{3/2}\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{q}}}}\le \log_{3/2}m$ credits per operation. During a deletion we also store an additional credit ``on the side.'' Thus, in total we give out at most $O(m\log m)$ credits. Even with these optimizations, there will always be sequences of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{delete}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operation for which a ScapegoatTree takes longer than other SSet implementations. This gap in performance is due to the fact that, unlike the other SSet implementations discussed in this book, a ScapegoatTree can spend a lot of time restructuring itself. \excref{scapegoat-nlogn} asks you to prove that there are sequences of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} operations in which a ScapegoatTree will spend on the order of $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}}$ time in calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{rebuild}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}}. This is in contrast to other SSet implementations discussed in this book, which only make $O(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ structural changes during a sequence of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}} operations. This is, unfortunately, a necessary consequence of the fact that a ScapegoatTree does all its restructuring by calls to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{rebuild}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} \cite{d90}. Despite their lack of performance, there are applications in which a ScapegoatTree could be the right choice. This would occur any time there is additional data associated with nodes that cannot be updated in constant time when a rotation is performed, but that can be updated during a \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{rebuild}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}} operation. content: \index{CountdownTree@CountdownTree} Analyze and implement a CountdownTree. In a CountdownTree each node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} keeps a \emph{timer} \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}. The \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations are exactly the same as in a standard BinarySearchTree except that, whenever one of these operations affects \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s subtree, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} is decremented. When $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}}=0$ the entire subtree rooted at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is rebuilt into a perfectly balanced binary search tree. When a node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is involved in a rebuilding operation (either because \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} is rebuilt or one of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s ancestors is rebuilt) \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{t}}}} is reset to $\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{size}(\ensuremath{\mathit{u}})}}/3$. Your analysis should show that operations on a CountdownTree run in $O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ amortized time. (Hint: First show that each node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} satisfies some version of a balance invariant.)

\index{DynamiteTree@DynamiteTree} Analyze and implement a DynamiteTree. In a DynamiteTree each node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} keeps tracks of the size of the subtree rooted at \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} in a variable \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{size}}}}. The \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{x}})}} operations are exactly the same as in a standard BinarySearchTree except that, whenever one of these operations affects a node \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}}'s subtree, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} \emph{explodes} with probability $1/\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}.\ensuremath{\mathit{size}}}}$. When \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{u}}}} explodes, its entire subtree is rebuilt into a perfectly balanced binary search tree. Your analysis should show that operations on a DynamiteTree run in $O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ expected time.

content: \exclabel{list-order-maintenance} \index{Sequence@Sequence} Design and implement a Sequence data structure that maintains a sequence (list) of elements. It supports these operations: \begin{itemize} \item \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{add\_after}(\ensuremath{\mathit{e}})}}: Add a new element after the element \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}} in the sequence. Return the newly added element. (If \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}} is null, the new element is added at the beginning of the sequence.) \item \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{remove}(\ensuremath{\mathit{e}})}}: Remove \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}} from the sequence. \item \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{test\_before}(\ensuremath{\mathit{e_1}},\ensuremath{\mathit{e_2}})}}: return \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{true}}}} if and only if \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e_1}}}} comes before \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e_2}}}} in the sequence. \end{itemize} The first two operations should run in $O(\log \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{n}}}})$ amortized time. The third operation should run in constant time. The Sequence data structure can be implemented by storing the elements in something like a ScapegoatTree, in the same order that they occur in the sequence. To implement \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{test\_before}(\ensuremath{\mathit{e_1}},\ensuremath{\mathit{e_2}})}} in constant time, each element \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}} is labelled with an integer that encodes the path from the root to \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e}}}}. In this way, \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathrm{test\_before}(\ensuremath{\mathit{e_1}},\ensuremath{\mathit{e_2}})}} can be implemented by comparing the labels of \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e_1}}}} and \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathit{e_2}}}}.
